country.comment: Primary ethnographic fieldwork was conducted in Mumbai (specifically K-East ward and the Mumbai Municipal Corporation / BMC), India; the author briefly cites secondary newspaper/literature examples from New York City and the Colorado River delta for comparison.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1 (p. 305); PDF p. 6 fn. 6; PDF p. 7 fn. 7; PDF p. 10 (p. 314)

effect_estimate.comment: Ethnographic qualitative study; numeric leakage percentages reported in the text (13.6%, 14%, 21%, 25%, 37%, 40%) are contested administrative/consultant water-audit figures rather than causal or statistical effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Exclusive Mumbai municipal water rules barred roughly one million settlers unable to document residence prior to 1995 from applying for formal water connections and gave recognized settlers smaller daily quotas on an intermittent schedule. A World Bank-supported water audit in K-East ward (2004–2007) generated contested leakage figures (40%, 14%, 21%, and 37%, compared with municipal figures of 25% and 13.6%) that municipal engineers discredited, stalling 24-7 supply and privatization reforms. In everyday practice, ward engineers governed via strategic ignorance, selective leak repair, and tacit tolerance of unauthorized connections and reconnections (even after court-ordered disconnections) mediated by local councilors, party workers, and plumbers, enabling formally excluded settlers to access municipal water as unrecorded 'leakage.'

mechanism_certainty.comment: Directly observed mechanism (level 2, the design ceiling for qualitative studies under CODEBOOK.md §9): the author directly accompanied ward engineer Patankar on field maintenance visits and observed in-office negotiations with a city councilor and party worker over tacitly permitted reconnection following a court-ordered disconnection, alongside direct review of contested audit documents and interviews with engineers and consultants.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 16–19 (pp. 320–323), Section 'Fixing Leaks'; PDF pp. 7–12 (pp. 311–316)

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines pre-1995 residency cutoff rules and unapproved settlement housing barring formal applications (ELIGIBILITY: documentation, tenure), street-level engineer 'strategic ignorance' and tacit tolerance of informal connections (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, accommodation), court-ordered pipe cuts and tacitly allowed reconnections mediated by councilors and party workers (ENFORCEMENT: disconnection, reconnection; political_coordination), and knowledge/authority divides across head-office planners, ward field engineers, and external consultants (institutional_fragmentation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, documentation, tenure, discretion, accommodation, disconnection, reconnection, political_coordination, institutional_fragmentation

outcome_flags.comment: Examines legal eligibility for formal connections vs. unauthorized connections (formal_connection), settlers' everyday access to municipal water via shared taps and leakages (water_access), smaller daily water quotas, per capita supply, and unaccounted/nonrevenue water volumes (service_quantity), and scheduled intermittent supply hours vs. proposed 24-7 continuous supply and repair shutoffs (service_continuity).

publication_year.comment: Published in Public Culture 27:2 with 2015 copyright date printed on the first page.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative ethnographic study based on participant observation, interviews, and document analysis; appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.

sample_size.comment: The paper does not report a numeric sample size of interviewees or field observations. It describes nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork in Mumbai focusing on the Water Distribution Improvement Project pilot in K-East ward (1 of Mumbai's 24 wards; population 806,360, area 28 sq km), drawing on interviews and participant observation with named engineers (Haresh, Patankar), unnamed senior municipal engineers, World Bank consultants, a city councilor, a party worker, maintenance crews, and residents.

study_design.comment: Anthropological/ethnographic fieldwork conducted over nearly two years combining participant observation (riding along with ward maintenance engineer and observing office negotiations), interviews with municipal water engineers and World Bank consultants, and review of municipal and consultant water-audit reports.
study_design.value: Ethnographic case study (participant observation, interviews with water engineers and consultants, and document analysis)
